The 'without performing a mutating call' property of the primitive, and the last failure mode: :347 'reports reachable:false for a 5xx response' stands up a second real HTTPS server answering 503 (:348-349 'const errorServer = createServer({ key: cert.keyPem, cert: cert.certPem }, (_req, res) => {' / 'res.writeHead(503);') and asserts :374-375 'expect(result.reachable).toBe(false);' / 'expect(result.status).toBe(503);' — a reachable-but-unhealthy endpoint is distinguished from an unreachable one. criteria.notes: 'Exercised directly against this package, ahead of 18/19/20's own doctor-check wiring' is the clause a reader might expect a cross-package proof for, and there is none — correctly. The suite lives in `packages/gateway` and imports only `probeConnectionReachability` from its own module; that IS the criterion's 'directly against this package'. The 'ahead of' half is a phase-time statement, checked against the tree rather than assumed: 18/19/20's doctor-check functions consume this primitive later (roadmap/16 §Interfaces produced quotes 19's own words, 'connection-reachability probe exercising 16's custom-CA path'), and nothing in this suite depends on them. One honest limitation of the fixture: because the fixture server is on loopback, the real SSRF guard refuses it, so every SUCCESS case in this file must inject a `buildClient` whose `resolveHostAddresses` answers a public placeholder (`203.0.113.7`) and whose transport dials the pinned loopback address back (:31-33 'function realNetworkSendRequestPinnedTo(pinnedAddress: string): typeof sendHttpRequest {' / 'return (req: HttpTransportRequest) => sendHttpRequest({ ...req, pinnedAddress });'). The file's own header (:15-29) says so. The consequence is that the SUCCESS path is proven against a real TLS handshake with a real CA but a stubbed name resolution; the two default-builder cases above are the ones that run the guard for real, and they prove refusal rather than success. That is a property of testing a loopback fixture against a guard designed to refuse loopback, not a weakened claim.

criteria.notes: Reconciled with what merged rather than re-derived, per `bddac4c` (PR #47) and roadmap/16 §Risks' PRECONDITION RECORDED 2026-08-01. The containment is NOT 'the flag defaults to false' — that phrasing was explicitly retired as 'true but soft'. It is that the wrap cannot be turned on at all: no MCP client in shipped source, no production construction or `setEnabled` caller, `.strict()` schema with no field, no environment variable, and a zero-arity worker-config builder. All five are the tripwire's five numbered `it()` blocks, and the tripwire was verified to fire against seeded violations rather than merely to pass. roadmap/16 §Risks additionally records that settling the 16/12 quarantine question is a PRECONDITION on any enabling work, so the tripwire failing CI is what sends an author to that bullet. Two honest limits on this tick. (a) `buildSimulatedWorkerMcpServers` is this package's own simulation of a worker config, exported from `index.ts` and consumed by nothing outside its two test files; the criterion's own word is 'simulated', and the real builder is cited above as a shape check. (b) The trailing clause 'only this phase's own native tools are worker-visible' is read in the context roadmap/16 §In scope gives it — 'no worker ever sees an upstream provider's MCP server, only this phase's own `tracker.*`/`observability.*` tools' — i.e. the contrast class is UPSTREAM PROVIDER tools. Read instead as a claim about the whole tool set it would be false at HEAD, because 11's and 12's tools are registered into this same server by design (criterion 6's second clause, ledger Gap 1's eight families). The load-bearing claim, and the one the evidence proves, is that no additional MCP SERVER appears.
